newsitem.title: UK: UK Ford workers face Liverpool job cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK Ford workers face Liverpool job cuts.

text.p: The U.S. car giant Ford Motor Co was poised on Thursday to axe a third of the 4,500-strong workforce at its Halewood plant in northern England.

British newspapers said Ford was set to announce sweeping job reductions and the end of volume car production at Halewood. They said the plant had lost a bid to produce Ford's new Escort model and production would be switched to Germany and Spain.
Workers at Ford's plants in Valencia, Spain and Saarlouis, Germany, have been promised they will build the new version of the Escort, ready for launch in 1998.
Unions and management were due to meet on Thursday to discuss Halewood's future and a statement was expected around midday (1200 GMT).
Ford declined to comment ahead of the meeting but workers said they expected the worst. Union leaders pledged to fight.

"My job today is to make it clear to the company that any threat of the partial or eventual total closure of this plant is unacceptable," said Tony Woodley, the Transport and General Workers Union's chief negotiator for the car industry.
"If the speculation is right, and I don't believe it is too wide of the mark, Ford are importing cars and exporting British workers' jobs. There is no justification for that at all."

Woodley blamed "slack" British labour laws for allowing Ford to cut jobs. "The fact that employee legal protection is the worst in Europe must not lead to Ford thinking it can take the easy option and discriminate against its UK workforce," he said

Roger Butler of the Amalgamated Engineering Union agreed. "We should be making cars in Britain for Britain," he said. "Without doubt one of the major issues is how cheap it is to sack people in Britain compared to Germany."

Butler said other British plants could be hit. "If the company can move its second best-selling vehicle then they can do it to any one of our plants in the UK. It is a threat to Ford of Britain and it has got to be stopped."
Workers arriving at the plant were in gloomy mood.
"I think it is a disgrace that work is being transferred from here to abroad," said production operator John Bohanna.

"There is no justification on the grounds of cost, with all respect to Spanish and German workers, to transfer work there," he said. "This country will be importing 130,000 cars a year -- and that is not acceptable."
